title: Teardrops on My Guitar
description: Taylor's breakthrough ballad about unrequited love for classmate Drew, who kept telling her about another girl. Its pop crossover made her a star beyond country radio.

pops.text: Yes, Drew was real! He was Taylor's Hendersonville High classmate, and she uses his actual first name right in the lyrics.
Drew sat next to Taylor in class and told her all about the girl he liked — never realizing Taylor was writing a song about him.
Taylor co-wrote this with Liz Rose, her go-to collaborator on the debut album. The idea hit her on the way home from school.
Producer Nathan Chapman layered mandolin, fiddle and hushed steel guitar for the country version — the pop remix swapped in a drum loop and dropped the banjo.
That guy in the video is Tyler Hilton from One Tree Hill. Taylor picked him partly because he actually resembled the real Drew.
Taylor insisted on filming at a real Nashville high school, Hume-Fogg, when the label wanted something more grown-up. Her brother, cousin and school friends play students in the halls.
This was Taylor's first real pop crossover: No. 13 on the Hot 100, No. 2 on Hot Country Songs, and top 10 on pop radio — a country teen crashing pop charts.
BMI named it Song of the Year at the 2008 BMI Country Awards, and it eventually went triple platinum in the US.
Plot twist: about two and a half years later, Drew showed up in Taylor's driveway. By then she was famous — and, in her telling, it was an awkward but civil hello.

title: Tim McGraw
description: Taylor's debut single, written in math class at 16 about a senior boyfriend leaving for college — and hoping a Tim McGraw song would make him remember her.

pops.text: This is where it all starts: Taylor's debut single, released June 19, 2006, when she was just 16.
She dreamed up the idea in math class, thinking about her senior boyfriend heading off to college, and had the song sketched in about 15 minutes.
She finished it that day with Liz Rose at a piano. Her favorite Tim McGraw song hidden in the lyric? 'Can't Tell Me Nothin'' from Live Like You Were Dying.
The original title was 'When You Think Tim McGraw.' Label head Scott Borchetta shortened it to 'Tim McGraw' — betting McGraw's own fans would get curious.
The cabin in this video belonged to Johnny Cash. It was filmed in Hendersonville, Tennessee, and premiered in July 2006.
The track rides the classic '50s progression — C, Am, F, G — the same doo-wop chord loop behind 'Heart and Soul,' with fiddle, mandolin and Dobro on top.
It climbed to No. 6 on Hot Country Songs and No. 40 on the Hot 100, after Taylor spent six months on a radio tour hand-sealing promo envelopes to stations.
The video won Breakthrough Video of the Year at the 2007 CMT Music Awards — Taylor's first major video trophy.
Full-circle moment: at the 2007 ACM Awards, teenage Taylor sang this song about Tim McGraw... directly to Tim McGraw, sitting in the front row.

title: Fearless
description: The title track of Taylor's second album — a song about the best first date she hadn't had yet, with a video stitched together from her first headlining tour.

pops.text: Taylor wrote this one while she wasn't dating anyone at all. She called it a song about 'the best first date I haven't had yet.'
She wrote it on tour opening for other country acts, with Liz Rose and Hillary Lindsey, while promoting her debut album.
Her definition became the album's motto: fearless doesn't mean unafraid or bulletproof — it means you have a lot of fears, but you jump anyway.
That's why she named the whole album Fearless after this song. It opens the record, too — track one, setting the theme.
No staged storyline here: this video, directed by Todd Cassetty, is built from Fearless Tour performances plus backstage footage from 2009-10.
On that tour she played this in a silver sparkly dress and black cowboy boots, twirling with a rhinestone-covered acoustic guitar — the look the Eras Tour later recreated.
As a promo single in fall 2008 it debuted at No. 9 on the Hot 100 — before it was even an official single. It later went platinum.
Taylor was the first woman since Madonna in 1998 to land two top-10 Hot 100 debuts in the same calendar year, with 'Fearless' and 'Change.'
The arrangement is powered by chiming 12-string guitars, mandolin and fiddle — then the bridge throws in a key change for that final lift.

title: Fifteen
description: A true story from freshman year about Taylor and her best friend Abigail Anderson — first loves, first heartbreak, and growing up faster than you expect at fifteen.

pops.text: This one is literally true: it's about Taylor and her real best friend, Abigail Anderson, surviving freshman year at Hendersonville High.
Taylor wrote it backwards — she started with the line 'Abigail gave everything she had to a boy who changed his mind' and built the whole song around it.
Before recording it, Taylor played it for Abigail and asked permission to use the personal details. Abigail said yes, hoping other girls could learn from it.
Taylor has said recording this made her cry, because it felt like watching someone she loved go through pain all over again.
Director Roman White refused to shoot in a real high school. Almost everything you see was created digitally around Taylor walking on a giant green screen for two days.
Abigail plays herself in the video. When Taylor is happy the animated garden blooms — when Abigail's heart breaks, clouds roll in and the garden dies.
Taylor performed 'Fifteen' as an acoustic duet with Miley Cyrus at the 2009 Grammy Awards, just the two of them on stools with a guitar.
It peaked at No. 23 on the Hot 100 and No. 7 on Hot Country Songs, won Choice Country Song at the Teen Choice Awards, and went double platinum.
The video was nominated for Best Female Video at the 2010 MTV VMAs — it lost to Lady Gaga's 'Bad Romance.'

title: Begin Again
description: Red's gentle closing track about daring to go on a first date again after a bad breakup — filmed as a love letter to Paris.

pops.text: On an album full of breakup chaos, this is the quiet ending: Red closes with the moment she dares to fall in love again.
Taylor previewed it on Good Morning America in September 2012, describing that shaky first date after you've dusted yourself off from a horrible breakup.
She wrote this one completely solo, and produced it with Nathan Chapman and Dann Huff. Listen for mandolin, banjo and steel guitar under the acoustic arpeggios.
That James Taylor lyric is no throwaway — critics heard Joni Mitchell and James Taylor's 70s soft-rock in the arrangement, and Taylor name-checks his records in the song.
Taylor called the Paris shoot a 'love letter' to the city. Director Philip Andelman filmed her wandering the Seine, cafes and bridges in a red dress.
The video changes the story a little: instead of the planned date from the lyrics, she has a chance meeting with a Frenchman while doodling in a Paris cafe.
It debuted at No. 7 on the Hot 100 and No. 1 on Hot Digital Songs, selling 299,000 downloads in its first week.
Critics singled it out for its maturity — Billboard put it at No. 6 on its best songs of 2012 list.
It earned a Grammy nomination for Best Country Song in 2014 — fitting for Red's most country-hearted moment.

title: Cruel Summer
description: Official audio only — no official music video was ever made for this Lover favorite. A secret summer romance from 2019 that fans willed into a No. 1 hit four years later on the Eras Tour.

pops.text: No official music video exists for this one — this is the official audio. Fans have been asking for a video since 2019.
Track two on Lover (2019), co-written with Jack Antonoff and St. Vincent — yes, Annie Clark plays guitar on it, too.
Taylor described it as a summer romance where you're yearning for something just out of reach — ecstasy, anxiety and pain all at once.
It's fast and fizzy: 170 beats per minute, wobbling synths and vocoder-treated vocals building to that long, wailing 'ooh' hook.
That bridge — 'I'm drunk in the back of the car' — was ranked No. 11 on Billboard's list of the best bridges of the 21st century.
Taylor revealed on the Eras Tour she had planned to make it a single in 2020, then scrapped the plan when the pandemic hit and she pivoted to Folklore.
The Eras Tour put it second in the show, it went viral, and Republic finally released it as a single in June 2023 — almost four years late.
It then spent four weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 in fall 2023, becoming Taylor's 10th No. 1 and Lover's first.
It became her longest-charting Hot 100 hit ever at 54 weeks, passing 'Anti-Hero' — not bad for a song that was never supposed to wait four years.

title: If I Could
description: A gentle Hoist ballad sung as a duet with bluegrass star Alison Krauss — Phish at their most tender, complete with a swelling string finish. Official studio audio via Phish - Topic.

pops.text: Trey Anastasio wrote this one entirely on his own, words and music — a rarity in a catalog usually co-written with lyricist Tom Marshall.
It's track three on Hoist, Phish's fifth studio album, released on Elektra Records on March 29, 1994.
That second voice joining Trey is Alison Krauss, then a rising bluegrass star, who sings a verse and adds harmonies throughout.
Trey and bassist Mike Gordon first caught Krauss live in Burlington and got obsessed; the band later saw her Hollywood show while recording Hoist nearby.
After that show, Phish talked Krauss into coming by the studio — and she nailed her vocal part in just two takes.
Krauss has performed the song live with Phish exactly once: May 3, 1994, at the Starwood Amphitheatre in Antioch, Tennessee.
Hear the strings take over in the final minute? That's a credited string section, the Richard Greene Fourteen, giving the ballad a Hollywood ending.
Hoist was produced by Paul Fox and recorded in late 1993 in Calabasas, California. It became Phish's best-selling album to that point, peaking at No. 34 and later going gold.
In December 2020, Trey and keyboardist Page McConnell released a stripped-down piano-and-guitar duo version as the opening track of their December EP.

title: Everything's Right
description: SWAP for 'David Bowie' (no verifiable official upload found). A modern Phish jam vehicle built on a singalong mantra — this is the band's official live performance video from Riviera Maya, Mexico, February 26, 2023.

pops.text: Lyrics are by longtime Phish collaborator Tom Marshall, with music by Trey Anastasio — and Trey's solo band actually played this song first, months before Phish did.
Phish debuted it on July 14, 2017 in Chicago to open their summer tour — and stretched the brand-new song into the first set's improvisational highlight.
The chorus is a pure mantra — 'Everything's right, so just hold tight' — engineered to be sung back by an entire arena.
It quickly grew into one of Phish's most reliable modern jam vehicles, with live versions regularly stretching past fifteen minutes.
This performance comes from February 26, 2023, the finale of Phish's Riviera Maya destination event in Mexico — a nineteen-minute ride.
Listen to the jam's mood swing: it starts in a dark, minor-key exploration, then flips into a blissful major-key groove just before the ten-minute mark.
The studio version on Sigma Oasis runs over twelve minutes — almost unheard of for Phish in the studio — because that album was recorded live in the room.
Sigma Oasis happened by accident: a November 2019 rehearsal week at Trey's Barn studio in Vermont turned into an album, which the band then rush-released the following spring.
Phish trusted this song to sell a show: a live 'Everything's Right' was the preview clip used to showcase their 2024 Las Vegas Sphere residency streams.

title: The Divided Sky
description: Phish's great composed epic — a mostly instrumental, multi-movement piece from their debut album Junta. This is a live performance video from the band's official channel, filmed June 1, 2022 in Charleston, South Carolina.

pops.text: This one's almost entirely instrumental — the whole lyric is essentially a single repeated line: 'Divided sky, the wind blows high.'
It comes from Junta, Phish's debut album, first sold on cassette at their shows in 1989 before Elektra Records reissued it in 1992.
Junta was recorded in 1988 at Euphoria Sound Studios in Revere, Massachusetts, with the four band members producing themselves.
An early version was already being played at Nectar's in Burlington in August 1987 — but it didn't have its middle section yet.
Fans call one intricate middle passage the 'Palindrome' section — a musical phrase built to mirror itself forwards and backwards.
It's often called the band's compositional masterpiece: a prog-style epic built from distinct movements instead of verses and choruses.
On Junta the track runs just under twelve minutes; live versions stretch much further — the famous Clifford Ball performance passes sixteen.
This video is the band's own official 4K performance, filmed June 1, 2022 at Credit One Stadium in Charleston, South Carolina.
In Phish's Gamehendge mythology, Divided Sky plays the role of grand finale — it closed the band's full Gamehendge performance at Great Woods in 1994.

title: Punch You in the Eye
description: A funky Gamehendge tale of a kayaker who washes up in evil King Wilson's kingdom — a song Phish never recorded in the studio, so every official version is live. This recording comes from the Phish: Ventura live box set, via Phish - Topic (JEMP Records).

pops.text: The narrator is a kayaker who accidentally washes ashore in the land of Wilson, the evil king of Phish's Gamehendge saga.
Wilson captures and tortures him — but the kayaker escapes, vowing revenge: 'Someday I'll kill you till you die.'
It premiered in October 1989. Careful, trivia hunters: an earlier, completely different 1987 song called 'Punch Me in the Eye' is not the same tune.
Buried in the middle is 'The Landlady,' a Latin-flavored instrumental that later escaped and lived a second life as a standalone song.
Page McConnell's nimble Cuban-style piano and Trey Anastasio's Santana-esque guitar are what drive the song's mambo-flavored middle section.
After 1989 the song vanished from setlists for over three years, finally returning on February 5, 1993 at New York's Roseland Ballroom — a gap of 414 shows.
At that Roseland comeback, Trey stopped the show to teach the crowd the 'Landlady dance' — also known as the Punch You in the Eye storm dance.
Phish never cut this song in a studio, so every official release of it is a live recording — including this one, from the band's Ventura live box set.
The little Landlady section became a fan obsession of its own: when it finally returned as a standalone song in 2015, it had been missing for 768 shows.

title: Dance Mode
description: The title track of Bluey: Dance Mode!, the second soundtrack album from the hit Australian kids' show — music composed by Joff Bush and the Bluey Music Team. The song shares its name with the beloved season 2 episode where Bingo wins the power to make her parents dance on command. Official audio via Bluey - Topic.

pops.text: 'Dance Mode' began as a Bluey episode — the very first episode of season two, which premiered in Australia in March 2020.
The whole adventure starts with a snack crime: Bandit eats the last of Bingo's chips — chips she was not actually finished with.
To make it up to her, Bingo wins a dangerous power: whenever anyone yells 'Dance Mode!', Mum and Dad have to dance — wherever they are.
The episode builds to Bandit dancing in a very public place, shouting to the crowd: 'Ladies and gentlemen, I'm doing this for my kid!'
All of Bluey's music is composed by Brisbane musician Joff Bush — who nearly turned the job down, thinking preschool TV wasn't for him.
Then Bush watched the first episodes and found himself in tears. He and the show's producer Daley Pearson were old music-school classmates, and he signed on.
This track is the title song of Bluey: Dance Mode!, the show's second soundtrack album from 2023, collecting seventeen songs from across all three seasons.
The album was a genuine hit: it topped Billboard's Kid Albums chart in the US and the UK's Soundtrack Albums chart.
Joff Bush's 'Dance Mode' won the Children's Music Award at the Queensland Music Awards — hometown honors for a Brisbane-made show.

title: Eyes Without a Face
description: Billy Idol slows down for a haunted ballad about a relationship rotting from the inside — and lands his first US Top 10 hit.

pops.text: That eerie title comes from a 1960 French horror film about a surgeon trying to rebuild his daughter's ruined face — all that was left of her was her eyes.
Idol has called this an anti-love song, written while his life in early-80s New York was sliding into infidelity and moral decay.
This was one of the first three songs Idol wrote for the Rebel Yell album, recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York with a Linn drum machine driving the pulse.
The ghostly French whisper in the chorus — 'Les yeux sans visage' — is Idol's girlfriend Perri Lister, a dancer who also turned up in his 'Hot in the City' video.
Guitarist Steve Stevens built the song on a slow revolving four-chord pattern, then detonated the middle with a hard-rock riff.
Over that riff, Idol suddenly starts rapping — he said rap was blasting in every New York disco and club at the time, so he talked streetwise over Stevens' barrage.
Released in 1984, this moody ballad climbed to No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the snarling punk's very first Top 10 hit in America.
Director David Mallet's surreal video put Idol singing inside a flaming hexagon surrounded by hooded figures, and MTV put it in heavy rotation.
The three-day video shoot literally hurt: Idol neglected his contact lenses so badly that he injured his eyes filming a song called 'Eyes Without a Face'.

title: Just Like Heaven
description: Robert Smith's dizzy love letter to Mary Poole — three and a half minutes of spinning, kissing and fainting that became The Cure's American breakthrough.

pops.text: Robert Smith wrote this about a trip to Beachy Head on England's south coast with his future wife Mary — he says it's about hyperventilating, kissing and fainting to the floor.
'Show me how you do that trick' reaches back to Smith's childhood love of magic tricks — and, he admits, to a seduction trick from later in life.
Smith disciplined himself to write 15 days a month for the Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me sessions in France, and this melody fell out of that regime.
Before the words were even finished, an instrumental version was already working — as the theme tune to the French TV show Les Enfants du Rock.
Drummer Boris Williams sped the demo up and added that opening drum fill, which gave Smith the idea to introduce each instrument one by one.
Smith knew the chord run resembled The Only Ones' 'Another Girl, Another Planet' — he has cheerfully admitted the similarity ever since.
Director Tim Pope rebuilt Beachy Head's cliffs inside Pinewood Studios for the video, shot in October 1987.
The woman dancing with Smith as the sky turns to night is Mary herself — the only woman ever featured in a Cure music video.
It peaked at only No. 40 in the US, but it was The Cure's first American hit — and in 2006 astronauts aboard Space Shuttle Discovery got it as a wake-up call.

title: Kiss
description: Prince took his own song back, deleted the bass, sang it in falsetto — and turned almost nothing into a No. 1 masterpiece of minimal funk.

pops.text: This was never meant to be a Prince hit: he gave it away to Mazarati, a funk band on his own Paisley Park label formed by his bassist Brownmark.
Prince's demo was barely a song — one verse, one chorus, simple acoustic chords, sung in his normal voice. Producer David Z thought it sounded like a folk song.
David Z rebuilt it in a single day, running a drum-machine hi-hat through a delay and gating an acoustic guitar to it to create that impossible, jerky funk rhythm.
Prince walked in the next morning, heard it, and took it back on the spot: 'This is too good for you guys. I'm taking it back.'
His edits were ruthless: he replaced the vocal with his own falsetto, added a James Brown 'Papa's Got a Brand New Bag' guitar lick — and deleted the bass line entirely.
Mazarati's backing vocals stayed on Prince's version, and that breathy 'ah-ah' hook was adapted from Brenda Lee's 1959 rockabilly hit 'Sweet Nothin's.'
The video, directed by Rebecca Blake, matches the minimalism: Prince in a cropped top dancing with a veiled Monique Mannen while Wendy Melvoin sits coolly strumming guitar.
'Kiss' spent two weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in April 1986 — Prince's third US chart-topper — and won a Grammy for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group.
Two years later Art of Noise and Tom Jones covered it and went one better in Britain, hitting No. 5 — one place higher than Prince's original managed there.

description: Billy Corgan looks back at being 12, bored and on the edge of growing up — a drum-machine daydream that became the Pumpkins' biggest US single.

pops.text: Billy Corgan wrote this from the perspective of his 12-year-old self in 1979 — old enough for a car and a job soon, still waiting for life to actually start.
He picked the year partly because it sang well — '1979' just flowed with the words he wanted to use.
This was the very last song finished for the 28-track double album Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness.
It nearly didn't make it: producer Flood dismissed the early version, gave Corgan about a day to save it, and Corgan rebuilt it overnight — some accounts say in about four hours.
Unlike the band's wall of guitars, '1979' floats on a drum machine, loops and samples — Corgan even manipulated his own voice into that strange recurring mutter you hear throughout.
The video, directed by Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris, follows suburban teens killing time — and every band member cameos, from James Iha's store clerk to Jimmy Chamberlin's policeman.
Disaster on set: after the shoot, the tapes were left on top of a car and lost forever as it drove off — the band had to fly back and re-shoot the house-party scene.
It peaked at No. 12 on the Billboard Hot 100, still the Pumpkins' highest-charting US single, and topped both the Mainstream and Modern Rock charts.
The video won Best Alternative Video at the 1996 MTV VMAs, and the band loved the characters so much they reunited most of the cast for a sequel — the 1998 video for 'Perfect.'
